# Evo II and W 196 R component airflow implementation proposal

Replace the Evo’s two whole-car airflow views with three experiments, **rear wing → front splitter → front wheel arch**. Replace the W 196 R centre-line tunnel with one **enclosed / exposed front wheel** experiment. The museum photo locates each part. Scrolling brings it into close-up. One tap should reveal something the air does, even with the animation paused.

The deliverable is four component steps, their offline data, English and Hungarian copy and tests. The Evo’s road-car comparison moves into its background note. The W 196 R’s straight-line estimate can go in its technical facts, labelled as a separate calculation. Both engine steps follow the airflow experiments. [Earlier proposal and figure](component-cfd-proposal.md) · [Evo stop](../stops/190e-evo2/car.js) · [W 196 R stop](../stops/w196r/car.js)

## Evidence to carry into implementation

| Finding from the current checkout | Implementation consequence |
| --- | --- |
| Compared with the Evo baseline, the 28 mm half-car mask changes **90 cells for the flap, 30 for the lip, zero for the arch**. At 40 mm the counts are **39, 26, zero**. All four published force-change flags for the lip are false. | The archived wing is a usable visual reference. The splitter needs a finer grid. The arch needs geometry that actually includes the flare and wheelhouse opening. Camera magnification preserves the original grid resolution. |
| Above the wing’s trailing edge, the mean air direction changes from **8.6° down to 4.0° up** on the 28 mm grid and **2.3° down to 5.7° up** on the 40 mm grid. | Put a direction arrow at the same physical patch in both settings. Keep the earlier model’s roughly **34 kg extra rear load and 9 kW extra drag power at 200 km/h** in the technical detail, explicitly attributed to the whole-car run. |
| The W 196 R body buttons produce identical **218 × 64** solid masks. Both use one vertical section between the wheels. Drag, area and mass inputs change in a separate road-load calculation. | Compute the air around the front corner in 3-D. A horizontal slice through those results can show air moving around the tyre. |
| The live solver uses a 2-D lattice, one side-profile mask, a moving road and stationary solid walls. The offline 3-D runner uses uniform inflow, a mirrored half-car, a simplified floor, stationary stepped tyres and a much lower Reynolds number than the vehicle. Its browser export contains two fixed scalar slices and pretraced paths. | Reuse the 2-D solver offline for the splitter and the 3-D kernel for the wing and wheels. Each new run covers the part and the adjacent geometry that shapes its flow. Export only the region the visitor sees. Treat the wing crop from the old full-car run as a prototype and cross-check. |

[Wing comparison image](evo-wing-flow-comparison.png) · [3-D geometry](../tools/cfd/geometry.mjs) · [Run settings](../tools/cfd/run.mjs) · [Published case metadata](../stops/190e-evo2/cfd/cfd.json) · [Current export](../tools/cfd/export.mjs) · [2-D solver](../lib/model/flow.js)

## Visitor interaction

| Step and default | Visitor action | Visible response and acceptance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Evo wing**, side view of the boot, wing and short wake. Start at baseline. | Switch **Baseline / Flap raised** for the existing illustrative geometry. | Keep the old flap position as a thin outline. A fixed box above the trailing edge contains a mean-flow arrow. The flap and arrow both change. The nearby streamlines make the upward turn readable while moving. |
| **Evo splitter**, road-level side view of bumper, lip and ground. Start retracted. | Switch **Lip in / Lip forward**. | A tick marks the original leading edge. Follow two air paths from ahead of the bumper, one passing above the lip and one below. The pressure shading uses one scale. If the setting difference is weak, use the travel mark for position and teach how each setting divides the air. |
| **Evo arch**, plan view over the outer front tyre shoulder. Start with the fitted flare. | Tap **Follow the air** to highlight a computed path. | Keep its starting point visible and trace where the air turns beside the wheel into the flank. Paused or with reduced motion, show the complete path with arrowheads. Add a slimmer reference contour as a second case only if it clears the same tyre and produces a repeatable, visible difference. |
| **W 196 R wheel**, wheel-height plan view. Start enclosed, matching the exhibit photo. | Switch **Enclosed / Exposed**. | Show the change in fairing shape and the slow-air wake together. A short line across the flow marks the same downstream station. Highlight where its speed falls below a fixed fraction of the inlet speed. The caption names the observed change in width or position. In the details, explain why the open car gave the driver a better view of the wheels in corners. |

Use one full-width view in phone portrait. Keep the camera, seed points, inlet speed, field range and guide position fixed when switching a pair. Changing component chooses a new camera. Keep **Pause airflow** available while either state is selected. Give the result a shape as well as a colour, and put the result sentence beside the control. Use the existing technical disclosure for the legend and model assumptions. Mercedes-Benz documents two front-spoiler positions and a retractable upper flap for the homologation Evo. The current model’s raised plate is an illustrative setting. [Mercedes-Benz on the Evo adjustments](https://media.mercedes-benz.com/en/article/4e61dcd8-fd75-47ca-830c-056734a165c2) · [Mercedes-Benz on the W 196 R body styles](https://media.mercedes-benz.com/en/article/b210a620-ecd7-42dc-b364-af3e85ff3d6c)

## Work order

Each row can be assigned as a separate coding task. The model suggestions indicate where numerical judgement matters. The wing exporter and renderer can be exercised together before a new solve finishes. Run the wheel case with the clearly distinct W 196 R bodies first, then reuse the working method for the subtler Evo flare.

| Task | Suggested owner | Input | Return for review |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A. Reproduce the baseline and export the wing crop | Sonnet, high | Existing Evo volumes | Two decoded crops, mask counts and signed wing probe angles on both grids |
| B. Implement playback and wire the Evo wing | Sonnet, high | A’s files and the contract below | Working baseline/raised/pause controls, EN/HU, two paused phone captures and a passing interaction test |
| C. Compute the local wing and splitter | Opus, medium | A’s wing reference, nose/wing geometry | Grid and time-window comparison for each part, compact fields, and the exact claim each supports |
| D. Compute W 196 R and Evo wheel flow | Opus, medium | Photo-based front-corner geometry and the 3-D kernel | Mask sections, matched-condition runs, wake comparison and the result for the optional arch toggle |
| E. Finish both stops and verify offline | Sonnet, high | B plus accepted C/D outputs | Final story order, bilingual copy, package sizes, targeted tests and mobile/offline results |

### A. Reproduce the wing reference

1. From the repo root check for `tools/cfd/evo2.glb` and `tools/cfd/out/{base,flap}-{28,40}.{json,bin,solid}`. The mesh and raw outputs are ignored by Git. This checkout has them. A clean checkout can run the published site from its committed assets. To regenerate a missing reference volume with the original mesh, use e.g. `node tools/cfd/run.mjs flap 28 9000`. Repeat only the missing case/grid pairs. Use the recorded mesh credit. If a required volume and the source mesh are both missing, mark the wing reference export pending. Exercise playback on the small test fixture while continuing the splitter and wheel work. Reproducing the off-centre probe requires the original velocity components. [Ignored inputs](../tools/cfd/.gitignore) · [Mesh source and transform](../tools/cfd/mesh.mjs)
2. Add an offline entry point, proposed as `tools/cfd/part.mjs`. Have `node tools/cfd/part.mjs wing reference` read the two base/flap pairs, sample the probe, and write the 28 mm display crop under the ignored `tools/cfd/out/wing-reference/`. Refactor the raw reader out of the existing exporter if sharing it. Importing it must have no write side effects. Keep the original whole-car commands usable. [Volume layout and reader](../tools/cfd/export.mjs)
3. In a raw 3-D file the four Float32 blocks are density, rearward velocity, lateral velocity and upward velocity. For `N = nx * ny * nz`, the cell offset is `(k * ny + j) * nx + i`. Its centre in mm is `[x0 - (i + 0.5)*h, (j + 0.5)*h, (k + 0.5)*h]`. Check for `16*N` bytes of field data and `N` mask bytes. Average the rearward and upward velocities over **x −3920…−3750, y 200…300, z 1230…1290 mm**. Compute `atan2(meanUp, meanRearward)` in degrees. Expect 48 fluid cells on the fine grid and 12 on the coarse grid, with the four angles above. Use actual rearward flow as the arrow’s horizontal direction.
4. Recreate the figure’s 28 mm crop by selecting cell centres in **x −4300…−3150 and z 810…1420 mm**, at **y = 238 mm**. This yields 41 columns × 22 rows. Its first column / bottom row centre is `[-3171, 238, 826]` mm. Colour by vertical speed divided by inlet speed, on the same −0.25…+0.25 range for both cases. Read the flap and boot outlines from the selected solid mask. Keep the full-precision volume for deriving the overlaid arrow and paths. [Reference image](evo-wing-flow-comparison.png)

### B. Build one component player and prove it with the wing

**Ownership.** Adapt `subsystems/race-aero.js` and its Evo configuration together. It already owns the precomputed case controls, theme mapping and tracer drawing, and the Evo is its only current caller. Reuse the same subsystem for each new part. Leave `subsystems/aero.js` serving the other stops. The story already supplies a step and an orbit target for each component. [Component loader and visibility](../lib/app/viewer.js) · [Story and disclosure layout](../lib/app/story.js) · [Current CFD player](../subsystems/race-aero.js)

**File contract.** Use one `field.json` and one `<case-id>.bin` per state under `stops/<slug>/cfd/<part>/`. Start with one scalar field per part. The manifest declares the plane, location, cell spacing, dimensions, scalar quantity, shared display range and case IDs. Each case carries its computed paths and guides in vehicle mm. Here is the wing reference header to use in the first round-trip test.

```json
{
  "plane": "xz",
  "originMm": [-3171, 238, 826],
  "cellMm": 28,
  "width": 41,
  "height": 22,
  "quantity": "vertical-speed-over-inlet",
  "range": [-0.25, 0.25],
  "cases": {
    "base": { "lines": [], "guides": [] },
    "flap": { "lines": [], "guides": [] }
  }
}
```

Rows run from bottom to top. Advancing a column always decreases vehicle x. Advancing a row increases z for `xz` or y for `xy`. The origin is the **centre of the first cell**. Use vertical velocity divided by inlet speed for the wing, pressure coefficient for the splitter, and mean-flow speed divided by inlet speed for the wheel views. Each binary is exactly `width * height` bytes in row-major order. Reserve 255 for solid. Quantize the common scalar range into 0…254 with rounding and clamping. Draw solid cells opaquely so the moving part remains legible. A path is an ordered array of `[x,y,z]` points. Give each guide a `kind` of `arrow` or `line` and a `points` array in the same frame. The fixture above illustrates the header. The display assets must contain the measured guide and the paths that the lesson uses. Keep labels in translated stop data. Keep run provenance, input geometry, both-grid results and raw units with the generation tools.

1. Start with `lib/model/part-field.js` and `tests/unit/part-field.test.mjs` for the pure format/mapping logic used by the exporter and player. A tiny asymmetric 3 × 2 fixture should catch a left/right mirror, row flip, misplaced half cell, bad byte count or solid decoded as a field value. Check both plane orientations, endpoints of the colour range, and the generated manifest’s case IDs against the stop config.
2. Reuse the stage’s camera, materials, `THREE.DataTexture` and existing path helpers. Share one texture and bounded geometry per component across taps. Use the same mm→m conversion on solids, paths and guides. Drive tracer positions from the exported mean-flow paths and elapsed time. The static field, mask and guide must remain readable at zero animation speed. Rebuild colours through CSS tokens on theme changes. One-sided velocity arrows must point aft on the car where rearward lattice velocity is positive. [Scene helpers](../lib/scene/helpers.js) · [Camera and theme API](../lib/scene/stage.js)
3. Use `params.data`, `params.start` and the existing `params.cases[{id,label,say}]` convention. Load the manifest and requested cases once per instance. Keep selection and pause state independent of fetch completion. On a rapid A → B → A switch, display the last selection. Apply the solid, field, paths, guide and result sentence as one state after data is ready. Check HTTP status and byte length. On failure show a translated message and allow retry, with the museum photo and story still usable. Return the normal `layout` / `update` pair. Show this group only when `active && !onPhoto`. Repeated story entries and settings changes must reuse or dispose GPU objects.
4. For the pilot, copy A’s verified `field.json`, `base.bin` and `flap.bin` together to `stops/190e-evo2/cfd/wing/`. In the Evo config replace the old racing step with `id: "wing"`, `subsystem: "race-aero"`, `data: "stops/190e-evo2/cfd/wing/"` and `start: "base"` (the last two in `params`). Supply `base` and `flap` labels and result sentences in both stop languages. Remove the separate autobahn step at this point and put its road-car figures into the background. Test this step with the wing-specific smoke assertion from E in the same change. When C passes, export the new wing cases to the same folder and update their provenance.
5. Use panel radio-style buttons with stable case IDs and `aria-pressed`, one pause toggle and a `text: { id, value }` result so the panel announces state changes. Start with stationary tracers under reduced motion. Store settings through the panel’s existing replay handlers. Keep them working when a language switch restores the selection before the assets finish loading. Set both component ghost opacities to zero for the model close-up. Keep photo identification and the closing photo outline in the existing viewer. [Panel API and state replay](../lib/app/panel.js)
6. Give the wing a near-side camera framing the boot edge, flap and short wake. For a first fit, try target `[-3.73, 0.238, 1.12]` and position `[-3.73, 1.88, 1.12]` in metres, then check both orientations. The side camera on +y puts downstream toward screen right. Set the camera on entering a step and let the visitor retain an orbit or zoom while comparing settings. Keep the archived result identified as a crop of the whole-car simulation until C supplies the local wing case.

**Done when** two paused stage captures show different flap outlines and different arrow directions at the same box. Check this before adding the other components. An updated button label alone is insufficient.

### C. Compute the local wing and splitter

**Repeatable offline runs.** Add the local cases behind `part.mjs`. A useful command contract is `node tools/cfd/part.mjs <wing|splitter|w196-wheel|evo-arch> <solve|export>`. These are proposed commands to implement. Each `solve` runs the component’s specified cases/grids into its own ignored output directory. Each `export` validates the complete case set, then publishes the compact display assets to its stop folder. Keep partial runs out of that folder. Check in the small geometry inputs and the generator, so regular builds and CI can use the committed exports without rerunning CFD. Preserve any external input’s source, assumptions and regeneration instructions.

**Local wing.** Build a domain around the wing, its gap above the boot, and the boot surface that feeds the gap. Resolve the hinged or extended portion from a documented profile or label the archived geometry as illustrative. Keep the baseline and changed geometries registered. Use the original full-car baseline’s upstream mean velocity profile to supply the same approach flow to both local runs. Save that small sampled inlet and its station with the case inputs. The current D3Q19 kernel initializes a uniform inlet. If extending it, accept a plane of inlet velocities, apply the existing equilibrium-distribution rule at fluid inlet cells, and retain the uniform default. Verify uniform-plane equivalence on a small grid. Keep enough upstream/downstream clearance for the measured turn to survive moving the boundaries. Compare the new local probe across grids and against A’s reference. If the local result disagrees, investigate inlet position, wing gap and resolution. Keep the archived crop labelled with its original run. [3-D solver](../tools/cfd/lbm3d.mjs)

**Splitter.** Draw two closed nose sections from the same bumper profile and ride height. Extend the lip longitudinally. The current 40 mm travel and 25 mm thickness are illustrative. Start at 5 mm per cell, which gives eight cells of travel and five through the plate, then repeat at finer spacing, for example 2.5 mm. Use `rasterize()` and `createTunnel()` from the existing 2-D model in Node. Allow fluid above and below the lip and continue the underside past the visible crop. Keep the road moving and the local domain larger than the on-screen view. Fix the model Reynolds number across refinements by scaling lattice viscosity with the feature length in cells at the same lattice inlet speed. Sample `cp(c)` on fluid cells beside each face over a stated chord interval and average over settled steps. Trace the two paths from fixed inlet seeds in the mean velocity field. Put the pressure map and old-edge tick in the export. If the face-pressure *change between settings* falls inside the variation, keep the position toggle and describe the visible upper/lower paths. Omit a front-axle load estimate. [Live solver functions](../lib/model/flow.js) · [Lip geometry](../tools/cfd/geometry.mjs)

### D. Compute the two front-wheel experiments

1. Build explicit local solids for the tyre, adjacent body, wheelhouse cavity and flare or fairing. Union the tyre and body only after carving the cavity. The existing filled-column Evo body would seal it. For the Evo use the front-wheel dimensions in `tools/cfd/geometry.mjs` as the starting point. For the W 196 R use the stop photo and body references for the two front-quarter shapes. Record assumed track, tyre and clearance dimensions. Inspect side, plan and cross-section masks before launching a long run. Check the road gap, connected air around the shoulder and a nonzero case-mask difference in the intended region. [Evo voxelizer](../tools/cfd/geometry.mjs) · [W 196 R frame and sources](../stops/w196r/car.js)
2. Use the existing offline 3-D kernel with the same road, inlet speed, yaw, wheel placement, outer boundary locations and tyre-motion model within each pair. Keep the current mirror at the vehicle centre by retaining the inboard strip of domain to y = 0. Cropping the rendered patch is inexpensive. Moving the numerical mirror onto the tyre shoulder would change the experiment. Start with a coarse geometry/debug solve. Refine until the smallest clearance or contour change relevant to the claim spans several cells. Budget 152 bytes per cell for the two D3Q19 population arrays alone before increasing resolution. Keep the region of interest away from the side and outlet boundaries. Run a larger domain once to check sensitivity.
3. Begin with stationary tyres over the moving road and label that simplification in both languages. The 3-D kernel supports a moving-wall term, but the current stepped spinning tyre pumped air artificially. A rotation-specific claim needs a resolved surface, contact treatment and a successful comparison to a moving-ground wheel benchmark. Match physical tyre-road clearance across the two grids. [Wheel modelling note](../tools/cfd/geometry.mjs) · [Experimental wheelhouse flow study](https://www.mdpi.com/1996-1073/12/17/3340)
4. **W 196 R.** Use one matched front wheel with the local exposed and enclosed body shapes. Choose a wheel-height `xy` plane and a downstream station in common exterior air, clear of both solids and the outlet. Fix these in physical mm before evaluating the final pair. As a starting definition, mark the connected band behind the shoulder where mean speed is below 80% of the inlet speed. Record its two lateral edges and width. Use the same threshold and search interval in both cases. Trace air from identical seed positions, export both outlines and wake guides, and have the text describe the observed direction. If the width is ambiguous, inspect the displacement and shape of the wake on the same plane. If neither repeats across grids, revise the domain or measurement and leave this comparison pending.
5. **Evo arch.** Seed a short ribbon just outside the front shoulder. In the fitted-arch case, export its path round the flare into the flank and measure its lateral displacement at a fixed station. For a comparison, change only the outer arch contour around the same tyre. Verify actual clearance on both grids. If the mask remains identical or the wake shift is unresolved, ship the validated fitted-arch path as a single-state lesson. **Follow the air** highlights that path and gives its one-sentence explanation. Label the narrower arch as an illustrative design experiment.

**Numerical acceptance for new runs.** Save the physical domain, spacing, boundary conditions, inlet speed, viscosity, settling time, sample region and reference velocity with each result. After the startup transient, take at least three successive time-window means spanning several flow-through times in total. In 3-D, `fields()` is cumulative over averaged steps. Difference successive weighted sums or accumulate the few local probes by window. Check finite fields, mask alignment and distinct local geometry, then compare the local observable across the two grids, time windows and an enlarged domain. Publish a directional comparison when its sign repeats and exceeds the observed window scatter on each grid. For a wake contour, repeat the check on its position or width and inspect the field itself. Keep the local result attached to the part. Whole-car drag, axle load and top speed each require a whole-car calculation.

### E. Integrate, localize and test the final stops

- **Stop data.** Use Evo component IDs `wing`, `splitter`, `wheel-arch`, then its existing `engine`. Use W 196 R component IDs `wheel`, then its existing `engine`. Point all four flow steps at `race-aero` with distinct data folders and component-specific `view`, `prompt`, `answer`, `more` and `talk`. Use `params.data` for the precomputed assets. The existing `params.flow` belongs to the live tunnel and its tests expect `params.shapes`. Move the Evo road figures into `note`, and label any W 196 R top-speed comparison as illustrative. Update the ledes, caveats, and sources to match each final run. Merge the aero edits into the current EN and HU arrays to preserve the W 196 R’s in-progress engine changes. Check remaining asset references before retiring the old whole-car display files.
- **Translations.** Mirror the English component order in both stops’ `hu.js` files. Keep component-specific `params.cases.*.label` and `.say` in these overlays. Use literal `t("…")` calls for common controls and loading states and add the matching catalog keys. For a new text field extend the translation test’s `TEXT` list. Keep case IDs independent of displayed strings. Check selection and pause after switching EN → HU → EN. [Translation coverage](../tests/unit/helpers.mjs) · [Catalog checks](../tests/unit/i18n.test.mjs)
- **Browser regressions.** The generic smoke test currently expects an `output` on every step and clicks the first case. With baseline selected that click does nothing. For the `race-aero` subsystem, assert the ready result, tap the *other* case, then assert the pressed state and changed result. For a single-state arch, tap **Follow the air** and check its visible result. Keep the moving-readout assertion for the other subsystems. Add a focused check for an actual stage change with the camera fixed and playback paused. Compare the same patch of fluid above the wing or downstream of the wheel, outside both solid masks and away from buttons. Also decode each exported field in the unit test and verify that the guide points in the direction of the recorded local result. A change in the bodywork alone must fail this check. Cover an immediate A → B → A switch, leaving/re-entering the step, reduced motion, failure/retry and language replay. [Smoke suite](../tests/e2e/smoke.spec.mjs) · [Step helpers](../tests/e2e/helpers.mjs)
- **Build and offline.** The build recursively includes `stops/` and stamps the worker with a content hash. Keep raw CFD outside shipped folders. Inspect the stamped precache for every new manifest and binary, and report the combined new byte count against the earlier Evo payload of 236,084 bytes. Extend the Chromium offline test to wait for **Ready offline** on the index, disable networking, cold-open both stops, enter every new step and exercise their controls. Wait for a case-specific result and inspect the changed field with networking disabled. [Build script](../tools/build.mjs) · [Offline test](../tests/e2e/offline.spec.mjs)

Run the following from the repo root. The new unit-test path and component IDs become available during implementation. The existing Playwright configuration starts a built site on port 8766. The optional screenshot helper uses the development server on 8765.

```sh
node --test tests/unit/flow.test.mjs tests/unit/part-field.test.mjs tests/unit/configs.test.mjs tests/unit/i18n.test.mjs
npm run e2e -- --project=iphone --grep '190e-evo2|w196r'
npm run e2e -- --project=chromium-offline
npm test
npm run e2e
```

For comparable desktop captures, start `npm run serve` in a second terminal. After B, use the proposed English button labels in the captures.

```sh
node tools/stop-shot.mjs 190e-evo2 wing /tmp/evo-wing-base.png 1000 'Pause airflow'
node tools/stop-shot.mjs 190e-evo2 wing /tmp/evo-wing-raised.png 1000 'Flap raised' 'Pause airflow'
```

**Final handoff.** Return one paired paused image per two-state lesson, one annotated path for a single-state arch, the two-grid observations, exact generation commands, input provenance, offline byte count and test results. On physical iPhone and iPad, check portrait and landscape, both themes, Hungarian wrapping, reduced motion and a cold offline opening. Ask a visitor to point to the change in the air with the details closed. Record which checks ran on hardware and which ran in emulation. If a local solve remains unresolved, identify the affected lesson and its last verified result.

# Component wind tunnels for the 190 E Evo II and W 196 R

Remove the Evo’s **Road car on the autobahn** CFD step. Move its road-car comparison into the background. Give the racing car three close-ups, beginning with the rear wing, followed by the splitter and the front wheel arch. Give the W 196 R one close-up of the front wheel in its two body styles. In both stops the museum photo locates the part, and the next scroll takes the visitor straight to the airflow.

## What the visitor sees

| Part | View and action | What to watch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Evo rear wing** | Side view of the boot lid, wing and a short stretch of wake. Start at the baseline and tap **Raise flap**. Keep a faint outline of the previous flap position. | A short arrow at a fixed point above the trailing edge tips upward. Air leaving the wing carries more upward momentum. The existing whole-car calculation gives the track consequence in the details, about **34 kg more rear load and 9 kW more drag power at 200 km/h** in this model. |
| **Evo front splitter** | Side section at road level. Keep the bumper, lip and road in frame. Tap **Lip in / Lip forward**. Show the starting edge with a small tick so the travel is immediately visible. | Follow air meeting the upper face and air passing through the gap below. Use the same pressure scale for both settings. Show a pressure difference across the lip only if the local run resolves it. If the two settings have a weak flow difference, teach how one lip divides the air with two labelled paths. |
| **Evo front wheel arch** | Look down on the tyre shoulder and the outside edge of the flared arch. Begin with **Follow the air**. Show a narrow ribbon entering beside the tyre, then trace it past the flare into the air beside the door. | The sideways turn around the shoulder is visible in plan. A fixed cross-section just behind the tyre can show where the slower air ends up. Add **Flared / Reference arch** only if a slimmer contour clears the same tyre and produces a repeatable difference. The reference would be a design experiment. |
| **W 196 R front wheel** | Match the photo by starting **Enclosed**. Tap **Exposed**. In a wheel-height plan section the streamlined fairing gives way to the front tyre. Retain a small section of the inboard body as a landmark. | Follow the slow air downstream. At one fixed station in the air behind the wheel, outline the region below the same speed threshold in both cases. The visitor can point to where the wake moves or changes width. Let the computed result set the caption. Follow the comparison with the driver’s trade-off. The streamliner suited fast tracks. Exposed front wheels helped drivers place the car in corners. |

Mercedes-Benz describes a two-position longitudinal front spoiler and a retractable upper rear flap on the homologation Evo. The current raised-flap geometry is illustrative. Use the exhibit photo and period drawings to establish the final part shapes. For the W 196 R, frame the comparison as a front-corner view of two distinct racing bodies. [Mercedes-Benz on the Evo adjustments](https://media.mercedes-benz.com/en/article/4e61dcd8-fd75-47ca-830c-056734a165c2) · [Mercedes-Benz on the W 196 R bodies](https://media.mercedes-benz.com/en/article/b210a620-ecd7-42dc-b364-af3e85ff3d6c)

## What the current tooling can show

![Two equal-scale crops of the computed wing flow. The baseline flap is flat. Raising it changes the mean air direction in the marked region from slightly downward to slightly upward.](evo-wing-flow-comparison.png)

**The wing can be prototyped now.** The figure comes from the saved 3-D velocity fields. On the 28 mm grid, the mean air direction in the box changes from about 9° down to 4° up. On the 40 mm grid it changes from about 2° down to 6° up. The box samples the same physical volume on both grids, 3.75–3.92 m behind the front axle, 1.23–1.29 m high and 0.20–0.30 m from the centre line. The arrows show the direction of the mean velocity projected into the side view. Both grids support the direction of change. Their different angles favour a simple arrow in the exhibit. The underlying Evo II mesh is by marksform (CC BY-NC 4.0). [Source mesh](https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/mercedes-benz-evolution-ii-190e-983f5e165dee4e7c801a49c33f8e76f1) · [Case generator](../tools/cfd/geometry.mjs) · [Solver outputs](../tools/cfd/run.mjs)

**The splitter and arch need new geometry at finer resolution.** I compared the saved half-car solid masks cell by cell. At 28 mm, the flap changes 90 cells, the 40 mm lip extension changes 30, and the arch trim changes zero. At 40 mm the counts are 39, 26 and zero. Every exported force change for the lip falls below the project’s reporting criterion. The current renderer marks the part on the same car outline, paints two fixed slices and moves dots along saved mean-flow paths. Zoom can reveal information in those fields, but the arch cases are geometrically identical. [Evo geometry](../tools/cfd/geometry.mjs) · [Force comparison and slice export](../tools/cfd/export.mjs) · [Current renderer](../subsystems/race-aero.js)

**The W 196 R comparison misses the wheels.** Both settings produce the same 218 × 64 solid mask. The speed readout changes because the straight-line model uses different assumed drag, area and mass. The live tunnel has a moving road and a stationary body polygon in a vertical plane. It can show air passing above and below a splitter. It has no sideways velocity for flow around a wheel. [W 196 R data](../stops/w196r/car.js) · [Tunnel selection](../subsystems/aero.js) · [2-D flow solver](../lib/model/flow.js)

## How to compute the close-ups

1. **Wing first.** Re-export the local mask and velocity patch from the saved Evo volumes to try the interaction shown above. The published files contain only two fixed speed/pressure slices and pretraced paths. The full velocity fields and source mesh are present in this checkout and excluded from Git. For a dedicated local run, keep the boot and wing gap and sample the incoming flow from the original car run. Check the local result against the existing wing trend. Keep the whole-car force figures attributed to the original calculation. [3-D exporter](../tools/cfd/export.mjs) · [Local CFD inputs](../tools/cfd/.gitignore)
2. **Splitter next.** Run the existing 2-D solver offline on two fine nose sections with the same road, bumper and ride height. A 5 mm trial grid gives eight cells across the illustrative 40 mm extension and five across its 25 mm thickness. Refine it and move the domain boundaries to check the pressure pattern. Export each settled field so the visitor sees the new state on the first tap. The local section can support a statement about pressure on the lip. Front axle load requires forces and pitching moment over the car. [2-D solver](../lib/model/flow.js) · [Current lip dimensions](../tools/cfd/geometry.mjs)
3. **Use the offline 3-D solver for both front corners.** Build the tyre, real wheelhouse cavity, adjacent flank and moving road. Keep tyre size, placement and inlet conditions fixed within each comparison. Allow air to pass on both sides of the outer shoulder. The current Evo tool fills body columns to a simplified floor and puts a stationary cylinder one cell above the road. Its rotating-wall option produced artificial pumping on the stepped tyre. Before showing wheel spin, verify a resolved rotating tyre against a moving-ground wheel benchmark. A stationary-wheel comparison can demonstrate the effect of the bodywork if labelled and checked on those terms. Verify the inlet and lateral boundary placement for the cropped domain. The existing runner assumes uniform inflow and a mirror at the vehicle centre. [Voxel geometry](../tools/cfd/geometry.mjs) · [3-D solver boundaries](../tools/cfd/lbm3d.mjs) · [Experimental wheel and wheelhouse comparison](https://www.mdpi.com/1996-1073/12/17/3340)

For each new case, inspect the solid mask before solving. Record the local quantity the visitor will see, such as the face-to-face pressure difference or the wake width at a fixed downstream station. Check its direction on two grids and its variation over multiple settled time windows. The present 3-D runs operate far below the car’s full-scale Reynolds number. A component run can support a local observation. Whole-car drag, axle load and top speed need their own evidence. [Run conditions](../tools/cfd/run.mjs) · [Current force reporting](../tools/cfd/export.mjs)

## Phone interaction and acceptance

Use the existing pinned story with a separate camera target for each part. Show one close-up at a time in portrait. Put the prompt, two named positions where applicable, and one sentence describing the result beside the stage. Switch the solid outline and its computed field together. Hold camera, inlet speed, colour range and tracer seeds fixed across settings. Keep an outline, a direction arrow or a wake contour visible when paused. Put pressure/speed choices and modelling notes in the existing detail disclosure. The same control and takeaway should fit in Hungarian. [Story steps](../lib/app/story.js) · [Viewer cameras](../lib/app/viewer.js) · [Panel controls](../lib/app/panel.js)

Serve compact paired fields and paths from the stop folders so the existing service worker caches them. Check a cold offline opening after the tour reports ready. On an iPhone, pause, switch settings and ask a visitor to point to what changed in the air before opening the details. Repeat with reduced motion and on iPad. If they can find the moving bodywork but need a number or a legend to find the airflow change, revise the view or teach the single-state effect. The wing figure demonstrates a local signal. The splitter and both wheel comparisons still need their local runs and device checks. [Offline build](../tools/build.mjs)

content.text:
Here is the problem written as a brief for a CFD specialist. I'd be sending them the numbers and the open questions, not asking for help with the code.

---

**Brief: lattice-Boltzmann close-ups for a museum explainer. Is the setup well-posed, and what can we claim?**

**Context.** This is a static website for the Mercedes-Benz Museum. Four exhibits get a precomputed airflow close-up, each showing two cases:
- 190 E Evo II rear-wing flap, down vs raised
- Evo II front splitter lip, in vs 40 mm forward
- Evo II front wheel arch (one state only)
- W 196 R front wheel, enclosed vs exposed

The claims are deliberately small: only the *sign* of a change, and only if it repeats on two grids. Computing is offline on one 10-core Mac, with our own Node.js solvers: about 16 M cell-updates/s in 2-D and about 30 M/s in 3-D. A fine-grid run takes 1–3 hours.

**Numerics, common to both solvers**
- BGK collision with Smagorinsky eddy viscosity (C_s = 0.16).
- Half-way bounce-back on the body. The road is a moving wall at u = U, in the car's frame.
- Free-slip top (3-D also free-slip side, and a mirror plane at the centreline).
- Inlet: equilibrium populations at ρ = 1, u = U, imposed every step, so density and velocity are both fixed.
- Outlet: zero-gradient (copies the last interior column).
- Reynolds number is held at a nominal value across grids by scaling ν with the cell size. Statistics: settle for several flow-throughs, then three averaging windows of one flow-through each.

**Problem 1 (main): 2-D splitter section (D2Q9)**
- **Geometry:** the centre-plane nose profile, traced from a photo. The body top is at 744 mm and the floor (ride height) at 120 mm; the lip is 25 mm thick. The body runs from the nose *through the outlet*, so it is effectively semi-infinite.
- **Domain:** 1.0 m ahead of the bumper face, 1.6 m behind it, 2.5 m tall. The body blocks about 30 % of the height, and the under-floor gap is a 120 mm channel driven by the moving road.
- **Parameters:** U = 0.1 (Ma ≈ 0.17); Re = 10⁴ on 1 m.
  - 5 mm cells: ν = 0.002, τ = 0.506.
  - 2.5 mm cells: ν = 0.004, τ = 0.512.
- **Observations:**
  - **Pressure level:** the interior sits 2–4 q∞ above the inlet density. Three cells behind the inlet there is already a vertical gradient of about 0.9 q∞. Referenced to the mean density at that inlet column (what our live tunnel uses), the lip's upper face reads cp ≈ 1.2 (not physically ≤ 1). So absolute cp is unusable.
  - **Drift:** the lower-face pressure keeps rising monotonically in every window. Lip in: 0.72 → 0.80 → 0.86. Lip forward: −0.16 → 0.02 → 0.18. The difference across the lip (upper minus lower, which needs no reference) is larger with the lip forward in every window, but that excess shrinks: 0.99 → 0.85 → 0.74. This was after 3 flow-throughs of settling.
  - **Failed variant:** ending the floor 0.5 m behind the bumper (a step up to 560 mm, open underneath) made the run diverge (NaN) within about 3 flow-throughs.
- **Questions:**
  1. Is the drift physical (the under-floor channel filling or emptying on a long time scale), or an artefact of the inlet fixing both ρ and u while the outlet pressure floats? Would a velocity inlet with free density (Zou–He), a pressure outlet, or a sponge zone fix the reference and the drift?
  2. What is the minimal well-posed 2-D section for a lip study?
     - Full-length car section with a closed tail and wake, versus a truncated body?
     - How far upstream should the inlet be, and how tall the domain, to keep blockage effects below the case-to-case difference?
  3. Is "upper minus lower face pressure, averaged over a fixed chord interval" a sound proxy for lip load? And is "sign agrees on both grids, and the change beats the drift between first and last window" a defensible stationarity test? If not, what is (a time scale estimate, a batch-means method)?

**Problem 2: 3-D front-corner tunnels (D3Q19, half car mirrored)**
- **Setup:**
  - U = 0.08, Re = 10⁴ on the 680 mm tyre diameter.
  - Cells of 24 mm (τ ≈ 0.5007) and 16 mm (τ ≈ 0.501), so the closure does essentially all the dissipation.
  - The tyre is still and lifted 48 mm above the road, so there is no contact-patch staircase; it is only 6–9 cells wide.
  - Domains are about 4.4 × 1.8 × 1.4 m (half width), so blockage is substantial; larger-domain runs are under way.
- **Metric:** width of the band where the time-mean |u| < 0.8U, on a fixed line at hub height 0.7 m behind the axle.
- **Results:**
  - W 196 R exposed: 574–806 mm (24 mm grid).
  - W 196 R enclosed: 830–870 mm (24 mm) and 826–858 mm (16 mm).
  - Evo arch: a path seeded in line with the tyre is shifted 377 mm outward at the station (24 mm grid); the three windows read 367–377 mm.
- **Questions:**
  4. At τ → 0.5 with this resolution, is a two-grid check at fixed *nominal* Re meaningful? The filter width scales with h, so the effective Re differs. What should be held fixed instead?
  5. Is the wake-width metric robust to blockage and to the still, lifted tyre? Would you pick a different observable for "enclosed vs exposed wheel"?

**Problem 3: what to compare**
6. **Evo arch:** the mesh's flared arch already sits at the tyre's outer face, and a narrower arch would expose the tyre, so there is no physical second case. Is there a meaningful variant at this resolution (for example, an open versus closed wheelhouse face), or is a single traced path the honest lesson?
7. **Wing:** the wing view is a crop of an earlier whole-car run (28 and 40 mm grids). The mean flow direction above the trailing edge goes from −8.6° to +4.0° on the 28 mm grid and from −2.3° to +5.7° on the 40 mm grid: the sign agrees, the size does not. Is a local wing solve with an inlet sampled from the whole-car field worth it, or is the sign the most this geometry (a game mesh) can support anyway?

**What we need back:** boundary-condition and domain changes for the 2-D section that remove the drift and fix the pressure reference; a defensible stationarity and grid criterion within a budget of a few CPU-hours per part; and a yes or no on whether each claimed sign is supportable.

Not quite. The flap and the lip are both adjustable, but neither moved while the car was driving: these were static settings, not active aerodynamics like a modern DRS.

- **Rear wing:** the upper flap could be raised or retracted. Evo magazine calls the trailing edge "manually adjustable", which means it was set on the car rather than worked by the driver.
- **Front spoiler:** the Mercedes-Benz article the stop cites says it "was adjustable in two stages in the longitudinal direction". So it has two fixed positions, further back or further forward.

So the similarity you noticed is right in one sense: both are settings chosen for a circuit. The difference is the range, from what the sources say: the front spoiler has two fixed stages, while no source gives a number of positions for the rear flap.

Two caveats from that Mercedes article:
- It doesn't say how either part was adjusted.
- It describes the road homologation car. Whether the DTM car used the same settings isn't stated.

The stop's text already handles the wing well: "an upper flap that teams could raise for circuits with fast bends". But "a front lip that slides forward" in the lede could suggest it moves while driving. I can add a sentence to the splitter step, in English and Hungarian: both parts are set before running, and neither is described as moving while driving. Do you want that?

content.text:
The review is right on the main points. It finds a real flaw in my splitter measurement, and shows that three of the four stop texts currently claim more than the runs support. I checked the splitter point against the code and it holds.

Note that the paste is a plan for drafting a reply, not the review itself. The underlying notes it cites are in `research_notes/Museum airflow claim review/`.

**What it tells me, step by step**

- **Splitter: the measurement is invalid.**
  - Both pressure probes cover x = 940–970 mm (`tools/cfd/part.mjs:97`), but with the lip in, the lip ends at 935 mm. In that case the probes sit in open air ahead of the lip, so the in-versus-forward comparison was never a lip load.
  - My stop text, "the lip is pressed down… larger with the lip forward", is unsupported and has to go.
  - The two 2.5 mm runs can't fix this, so they're wasting about 2 machine-hours.
  - A real answer needs proper boundaries: a velocity inlet with free density, a pressure outlet, and a sponge. It also needs a finite car section where the air over and under rejoins before the outlet, and the force summed over the lip's actual surfaces. That's a proper project, not a tweak.
- **Wing: the claim holds, but the wording is too strong.** Raising the flap tips the air upward by +12.6° on one grid and +8.0° on the other. The "from 9° down to 4° up" reversal depends on where the box is placed, so the text should say the air tips upward by roughly 8–13°.
- **W 196 R: no two-grid result yet.**
  - The 23 cm versus 4 cm figures are coarse-grid only.
  - The enclosed "4 cm layer" is mostly the first usable cell beside the body wall, so it measures my threshold more than the air.
  - It still needs the fine exposed run and a larger-domain check of both cases.
  - A better metric is the integrated speed deficit over a common patch of air, not a band width set by a threshold.
- **Evo arch: fine as a one-state illustration, with two wording fixes.**
  - Call the line a path of the mean flow, not where one parcel of air goes.
  - Don't credit the 37 cm outward shift to the flare, since no run separates the flare from the rest of the front corner.

**Release rule it proposes.** Keep the physical geometry, Reynolds number and probe location fixed. Average over independent batches. Require each grid's 95 % interval for the change to sit on the same side of zero, and the domain-size effect to be smaller than the change. If the budget runs out first, label the sign "unresolved". That replaces my ad-hoc "sign repeats and beats the drift" rule.

**What I'd do now**

1. **Stop the splitter 2.5 mm runs.** That frees the CPU for the W 196 R and arch runs.
2. **Splitter:** keep the step as the proposal's fallback, showing how the lip divides the air. Remove all load claims and say no load sign is given.
3. **Rewrite the wing, wheel and arch texts in both languages** along the lines above. Until the W 196 R checks pass, the wheel text describes the coarse picture without a confirmed difference.
4. **Wheel checks:** add the enclosed larger-domain run and switch to the deficit metric with the 95 % gate.
5. **Proper splitter tunnel:** leave it as an open item for you to decide on. It would change or fork `lib/model/flow.js`, which the live tunnels on other stops also use.

Shall I go ahead with 1–4?

git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Show the Evo II and W 196 R airflow one part at a time

The Evo II's whole-car wind tunnel gives way to three precomputed close-ups
(wing, splitter, wheel arch) and the W 196 R gets a front-wheel close-up,
played by the new race-aero subsystem from per-part field files made by
tools/cfd/part.mjs (about 107 kB in all, against 236 kB before).

Claims follow an expert review: a sign is stated only when the 95 %
interval over one-flow-through batches lies on one side of zero on both
grids and a larger tunnel moves it less than the effect. Wing: only the
change the flap makes. Splitter: display only. W 196 R: the wake behind
the bare tyre (61 % and 44 % speed loss on the 24 and 16 mm grids); the
air beside the car did not settle and is not claimed. Evo arch: one grid,
a path of the mean flow.

Also includes in-progress work on several stops, the crank-twist model,
real-part photos, research notes and proposals.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
